newsitem.title: CANADA: Surf corporate "cool" for fun and advice.
newsitem.headline: Surf corporate "cool" for fun and advice.

text.p: Two feet planted on the board and ready to give into the temptation of surfing to a few of those self-proclaimed "cool" sites that can be found all over the World Wide Web.

The research firm Dataquest, of San Jose, Calif., recently found that the majority of people surfing the Web spend/waste/enjoy 6.6 hours, or 68 minutes on the average single session, out on the Internet each week.

Where they go is anybody's guess, but there should be no doubt that the commercial sites with their banner ads and expensive graphics have been trying hard to attract repeat visits. Maintaining a list of the latest "cool" Web sites seemed to be the most popular way of tantalizing surfers to come back for more.
So, revved my ISP (Internet Service Provider, don't you know?) and after a few clicks, modems squawks and balks, we were up and running.
Ditched the Enterprise home page (http://www.enterprise.ca) after finding their mystery recommendation for the day: http://www.unitedmedia.com.
The bytes started chugging in and the suspense was building. Where had they sent me? To the land of Star Trek? The CIA's home page? The Library of Congress?
Ah, what a relief; it's comic relief. "You've uncovered the Web's largest collection of comic strips and editorial cartoons!" said the greeting.

There were Dilbert and Peanuts comic strips and of course there was commercialism -- par for the course on the Web in 1996 -- where one could buy books and the like. It was all offered by United Media, "a global syndication and licensing organization based in New York City."

For fanatics of the droll Dilbert and his life in today's zany corporate world there was no shortage of trivia provided by author Scott Adams. One area was, "Early photos of me (may frighten young children)" while another department was entitled "shameless self-promotion."
An added bonus, however, was Adams' electronic mail address (scottadams@aol.com) where one could provide grist for future cartoons by onpassing some gems from one's own corporate cubicle.

Now on the Web all good things come to end quickly so we jumped to the Yahoo search engine which was offering a site they said was a top pick from other surfers: http://www.izzy.net/vnestico/t-market.html.
Clicked to make the jump. But Whoa! How many bytes was that coming my way? Tedium in warp drive as the picture slowly came into focus. How long could we wait?
But in the end it was worth it. It was a page dedicated to helping others fight off telemarketers.

It provided some sage advice: "Never buy anything from a telemarketer! Telemarketers trade lists of numbers that they were successful with, or those who showed interest. You don't want to be on one of those lists!"

So far the sites had been fun and informative, but perhaps a little something more meaningful was needed for the brain. Perhaps a site whose visitors number in the low thousands and not likely a top pick of too many "cool" lists.
It was found among the bookmarks; a page dedicated to the writings of futurist and Wired magazine favorite George Gilder (http://homepage.seas.upenn.edu/gaj1/ggindex.html).

Gilder has tucked away some good reads from stories he wrote for Forbes' ASAP magazine. Not burdened by graphics and other doodads, the page honed in quickly. We clicked on, INTO THE FIBERSPHERE, among a list of stimulating subjects.
There was a catchy beginning to the essay on networks: "In a world of dumb terminals and telephones, networks had to be smart. But in a world of smart terminals, networks have to be dumb."

It was something to be savored for later because it was again time to get back on to the board. We surfed over to Excite and bounced to their offerings of the top 100 sites (http://www.100hot.com/). But, alas, far too many choices so instead decided to zoom to a zone with far less options, "Today's Cool Site (http://cool.infi.net/index.html). Just to be different, picked July and saw a sure crowd pleaser: a home page for British humorist Monty Python (http://www.PythOnline.com/).

A few bawdy openers but then avenues for a lot of Python humor, including "The Spam Club," "Games," and even "Shopping." But curiously the computer couldn't find a hyper link to escape the main page. The computer's fault or Python style humor?
Well, the answer was not forthcoming and modem and computer were looking tired. It was time to quit the voyage as one can only encompass only so much "coolness" in one session. Surfer at rest.
(To comment on this weekly column, Russell Blinch can be reached at: russell.blinch@reuters.com)
